comparisons.interpretation: Both support John Lewis voting-rights protections; Hoyer emphasizes his claimed House record while Crooms also names the Freedom to Vote Act and cybersecurity.
Both support John Lewis voting-rights legislation. Their additional election-reform proposals differ without establishing opposition.

Crooms emphasizes a Green New Deal and local green industry centered on working people; Hoyer emphasizes implementing enacted federal investments and environmental protections. No rejection of the other's approach is inferred.

Crooms names a Green New Deal and green industrial investment; Bareebe names renewables, nuclear energy, transit incentives and polluter penalties. The source does not establish Crooms's position on nuclear power.

Both support an assault-weapons ban, although Crooms specifies additional magazine and background-check provisions and Hoyer invokes reinstating the 1994 law. Shared support does not imply identical statutory definitions.
Both combine legal pathways with enforcement. Crooms emphasizes work visas, employer accountability and humanitarian access; Hoyer emphasizes border security and DREAMers. These elements can coexist.

Crooms describes citizenship paths for workers and people facing danger, alongside visa and employer rules. Bareebe specifies work, tax and felony-record conditions for undocumented residents' legal status. The proposals address overlapping but not identical populations and statuses.
Crooms emphasizes professional and public-service expertise oriented toward working people; Hoyer emphasizes legislative leadership and delivery of federal projects and laws.

Crooms presents public-sector legal and environmental expertise; Bareebe presents financial management and care-business experience. These are their stated qualifications rather than independent assessments of competence.
